cards.explanation: The answer is False. It takes more than one witness. Paul says, “Every matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses.” The rule comes from Deuteronomy 19:15, and he brings it up right as he's about to visit. Two or three witnesses is a sturdy table, and one witness is a table with one wobbly leg.

The answer is False. Paul goes easy on no one. He warns “…those who sinned earlier and everyone else: If I return, I will not spare anyone…” He says it to the ones who sinned and to everybody else. That's a warning aimed at the whole room, so nobody can pretend it was meant for the person sitting next to them.

The answer is that Christ is speaking through Paul. Paul says they are “…demanding proof that Christ is speaking through me.” Then he adds that Christ “…is not weak in dealing with you but is powerful among you.” They asked for proof, friends, and he points them to Christ.

The answers are weakness and power. Paul writes, “For He was indeed crucified in weakness, yet He lives by God’s power.” The cross looked like weakness, and Paul says it plainly. I like that he doesn't dress it up. The same sentence that says weakness says power, and that's what Paul wants them to hear. In that very verse he adds that he and his companions are weak in Him, yet by God’s power they will live with Him concerning the Corinthians.

The answer is whether they are in the faith. Paul says, “Examine yourselves to see whether you are in the faith; test yourselves.” They had been demanding proof from him, and now he turns the question back to them. Funny how the clipboard changes hands.

The answer is that Paul's group appears to have failed. That's a generous prayer. Paul says they pray “…that you will do what is right, even if we appear to have failed.” He'd rather the Corinthians do right than have his group look good. I'd take looking bad over a ruined batch any day, and Paul seems to agree.

The word is strong. Paul writes, “…we rejoice when we are weak but you are strong…” He says his group is weak, and they rejoice when the Corinthians are strong. That's a leader cheering from the back of the room, and I love it.

The answer is to build the Corinthians up. Paul says the Lord gave him authority “…for building you up, not for tearing you down.” That's the whole job description, friends. A tool made for building doesn't do much good when it's swung like a wrecking ball.

The answer is to aim for perfect harmony and live in peace. Paul says, “Aim for perfect harmony, encourage one another, be of one mind, live in peace.” Four short things in a row, easy to remember and hard to do. Anybody who's tried to get a whole group to agree on one thing knows that harmony takes aim.

The answer is True. Right after the list, Paul says, “And the God of love and peace will be with you.” He tells them what to do, and then he tells them who will be with them. That's a good way to send somebody off.

The answer is the fellowship of the Holy Spirit. Paul closes with “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with all of you.” The Lord Jesus Christ, God and the Holy Spirit are all named in one line. What a way to end a letter.

The answer is False. The last line is for everyone. Paul closes with “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with all of you.” The words are all of you. I'd say that's a pretty big blessing to end on.
